query: What should an investigator check when a new device makes a large payment?

results.title: Playbook — Account Takeover From A New Device
results.text: Playbook: Account takeover from a new device Overview: An attacker gains control of the customer's mobile or internet banking, registers a new device and quickly drains the account through high-value payments to new payees. Detection signals: - First login from a device never seen on the account. - UPI PIN reset or password reset minutes before the payment. - High-value payment to a beneficiary added the same day. - Login location far from the customer's usual city. - Transaction at an unusual hour for this customer. - Old device still active in the same period. What the investigator should check: 1) Compare the device fingerprint with the customer's device history. 2) Check the time gap between device registration, PIN reset and payment. 3) Check whether the registered mobile number or email changed recently. 4) Call the customer on the number held before any recent change.

Limited liability: When the customer reports a third-party breach between four and seven working days after the alert, liability is limited to the transaction value or a fixed cap, whichever is lower. The cap depends on the account type: about five thousand rupees for basic savings accounts, ten thousand rupees for most savings accounts and smaller credit cards, and twenty-five thousand rupees for current accounts and higher-limit credit cards. Reports made after seven working days are handled under the bank's board-approved policy. 4. Any loss after the report is borne by the bank.

results.title: RBI — Customer Liability In Unauthorised Electronic Banking Transactions
results.text: Issuer: RBI 1. Purpose: This guidance sets out how much of a loss a customer bears when money leaves their account through an electronic transaction they did not authorise. It covers internet banking, mobile banking, UPI, card-present and card-not-present transactions, and prepaid instruments issued by banks. The aim is to give customers confidence in digital channels while making banks responsible for the security of the systems they run. 2. Zero liability: A customer has zero liability when the unauthorised transaction happened because of contributory fraud, negligence or a deficiency on the part of the bank, whether or not the customer reported it. A customer also has zero liability when the breach lies elsewhere in the system, neither with the bank nor with the customer, provided the customer tells the bank within three working days of receiving the transaction alert.

Bank obligations: The bank must credit the disputed amount to the customer's account as a shadow reversal within ten working days of the report, without waiting for an insurance claim. query: How do we spot an account that receives money from many victims and moves it out quickly?

results.title: Playbook — Mule Account Receiving Fraud Proceeds
results.text: Playbook: Mule account receiving fraud proceeds Overview: An account receives money from many unrelated victims and moves it out within minutes to other accounts, wallets or cash withdrawals. Detection signals: - Many inward credits from unrelated remitters in a short time. - Outward transfers within minutes of each credit. - Account recently opened or long dormant and suddenly active. - Balance kept close to zero. - Same device or IP used by other flagged accounts. - Complaints on the national cybercrime portal naming the account. What the investigator should check: 1) Calculate inflow-outflow ratio and average holding time. 2) Map onward transfers to find the next layer. 3) Check whether the account holder's profile matches the volume. 4) Check the business correspondent or branch that opened the account. Containment and next steps: - Debit-freeze the account under policy.

results.title: Playbook — Job Scam Used To Recruit Mules
results.text: Playbook: Job scam used to recruit mules Overview: Victims are offered part-time work such as 'payment processing' or 'rating products' and are asked to receive and forward money through their accounts. Detection signals: - Customer says they were offered a work-from-home job. - Regular inflows followed by forwarding to the same set of accounts. - Messages mention commission on each transfer. - Young customer with a new account and sudden high volume. What the investigator should check: 1) Interview the account holder about how they got the job. 2) Identify the accounts they forwarded money to. 3) Check social media or messaging handles they were contacted through. Containment and next steps: - Restrict the account and explain the legal risk to the holder. - Report the recruiter's accounts and handles. Evidence to keep:

results.title: RBI — Mule Accounts And Their Detection
results.text: Issuer: RBI 1. What a mule account is: A mule account is a bank account used to receive and move the proceeds of fraud. The holder may be complicit, may have rented the account for a fee, or may be unaware that their KYC was misused. Mule networks let fraudsters break the money trail across many accounts and banks. 2. Detection: Banks are encouraged to use data analytics and machine learning models to spot mule accounts. Typical features include account age, the ratio of inward to outward flows, the number of unique remitters, time between credit and debit, device sharing across accounts and links to complaints on the national cybercrime portal. 3. Action: Suspected mule accounts should be frozen or debit-restricted following the bank's policy, the holder should be contacted for an explanation, and the case should be reported.

results.text: Playbook: QR code and 'scan to receive' scam Overview: The fraudster sends a QR code or payment link claiming the victim will receive money, for example for an item they are selling online. Scanning and entering the PIN sends money instead. results.title: Playbook — Sim Swap Fraud
results.text: Playbook: SIM swap fraud Overview: The attacker gets a duplicate SIM for the victim's number, receives OTPs and re-registers banking apps on their own phone. Detection signals: - Customer's phone suddenly loses network. - Telecom operator reports a recent SIM change. - UPI re-registration on a new device right after the SIM change. - OTPs delivered while the customer says their phone had no signal. - Several transactions in quick succession after re-registration. What the investigator should check: 1) Query the telecom SIM-change date through the available API. 2) Match the time of SIM change with the device registration. 3) Check whether the customer's email was also changed. 4) Check the KYC documents used for the duplicate SIM if police request them. Containment and next steps: - Block all digital channels until the customer is re-verified.

query: Customer shared an OTP with a caller pretending to be from the bank

results.title: Investigator Note SEN-2026-41194
results.text: Case SEN-2026-41194 | Typology suspected: OTP phishing and vishing | Status: Confirmed fraud Summary: Alert raised by the real-time rules engine. Customer is based in Ahmedabad. Disputed amount Rs 230,949 via internet banking at 14:30. Session originated from Indore on Android device (Samsung). Observations: Noted customer reports a call from someone claiming to be bank staff. Noted card-not-present transaction at a merchant the customer never used. Checks performed: I looked for other customers reporting the same caller number. I listened to or read the customer's account of the call and note the script. I checked whether the OTP was entered from the customer's device or elsewhere. Outcome: Fraud confirmed. Partial funds frozen at the beneficiary bank; remaining amount had already moved to a second-layer account.
